source.title: Scaling the Wild: Decentralizing Hogwild!-style Shared-memory SGD
source.authors: Bapi Chatterjee; V. Kungurtsev; Martin Jaggi

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares held-out accuracy across batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets, using distributed training methods rather than the original large-batch studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that larger local batches degrade test accuracy for MB-SGD and PL-SGD in several settings; its asynchronous methods often retain or improve accuracy. It also reports a LARS comparison. These results bear on V5. Rows below record test accuracy from the cited result tables; training accuracy and losses are omitted because V5 concerns held-out performance.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out accuracy at different local batch sizes under equal epoch budgets in distributed SGD, testing V5. It is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the reported large-local-batch degradation, but overstates consistency. The authors conclude that their asynchronous methods improve throughput with competitive accuracy, and that system-generated noise improves generalization in some cases. Some asynchronous results slightly underperform their small-batch references. The noise explanation is heuristic, not an isolated causal finding.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies decentralized asynchronous SGD and partial backpropagation with image classifiers, rather than the original large-batch comparisons; training duration is held to an equal number of epochs across methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome differs by training method and local batch size; the CIFAR-10 WIDERESNET-16x8 comparison also varies the number of workers. The paper says LARS did not help MB-SGD or PL-SGD check poor generalization at larger batch.

fits_no_version.finding: LAP-SGD and LPP-SGD often retain or improve accuracy while accelerating training, using smaller local batches and different learning-rate schedules.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Asynchronous distributed training can improve throughput while retaining small-local-batch accuracy; these comparisons do not demonstrate elimination of a penalty at the same enlarged batch.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 7 and Appendix B offer noise and escape-time explanations for generalization, without measuring magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Asynchrony and periodic averaging may favor generalization through altered noise and basin escape dynamics.

record.problems: Several reported comparisons do not state uncertainty; the text says results are means of 3 runs unless otherwise mentioned, and Table 9 reports means of 5 runs. The study focuses on its own asynchronous methods and does not directly establish a general critical batch size.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1, 5, 6, 7, 11, and 12 also report held-out accuracies for asynchronous methods and additional batch-size configurations. The selected rows prioritize the standard MB-SGD/PL-SGD batch comparisons and the LARS result; detailed asynchronous-method rows were omitted because the paper’s text summarizes them as recovering or improving baseline results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out generalization.
Width variation beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; LARS here does not supply that comparison.

Language models, longer-training remedies, normalization or regularization remedies, and systematic estimation of workload-dependent batch thresholds. The asynchronous comparisons do not establish recovery at the same enlarged local batch.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, generalization-gap correlations, and rankings against norm or margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random removals.

missing.what: Table 9 reports PL-SGD with LARS, local batch 1024, test accuracy 84.69% and training accuracy 93.67%, averaged over five runs. Compare cautiously with Table 1's 92.98% small-batch PL-SGD accuracy; there is no matched small-batch LARS control. Table 9 omissions are not declared in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's empty-evidence limits_scope verdict: maintaining accuracy with smaller local batches does not establish recovery at enlarged local batches, and untested workloads are not scope failures. Default results are three-run means; dispersion and significance tests are not reported. For synchronous MB-SGD, global batch equals local batch times worker count; PL-SGD uses local updates and periodic model averaging. Substantial training-accuracy losses in several large-batch runs mean these results need not represent a pure generalization-gap increase at equal training fit.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence were not tested.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold was not varied.
Convolutional and fully connected architectures were not compared.

The study tests image classifiers, not language models; it does not establish a workload-dependent critical batch size generally. Its asynchronous methods and some configurations do not show a large-batch penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures were not tested.
Memorized examples were not identified or removed.
